title: Photosynthesis explained simply
subtitle: Plants & energy
subject: sciences
description: Plants do something extraordinary: they cook sugar with light, water and air. And they give us oxygen as a gift.

hero.hook: A leaf is a solar kitchen: light, water, air... and here's sugar.

blocks.text: Imagine a miniature plant in each leaf. It takes three mundane ingredients: **light from the Sun**, **water** from the roots and **CO₂** from the air. It comes out with **sugar** to grow, and releases **oxygen**.
This feat is called **photosynthesis**. Without it, no forests, no breathable oxygen, almost no complex life on Earth.

sections.title: Where does it happen in the sheet?

blocks.text: In the plant cell, green organelles, the **chloroplasts**, house the . This pigment mainly captures the blue and red of light. Green is returned: this is why the leaves appear green to us. [[Chlorophyll]]

The simple equation: CO₂ + water + light → sugar + oxygen. The gas enters through tiny pores, the . Water rises from the roots. Sugar becomes wood, fruit, roots; the oxygen goes into the air. [[stomata]]
Chlorophyll “refuses” green. She prefers blue and red, more effective for exciting her electrons and launching the energy machine.
First, the **light phase**. Light breaks up water molecules. Oxygen escapes. Energy is stored in two chemical “batteries,” the **ATP** and the **NADPH**.

Next, the **manufacturing phase**, the [[The Calvin cycle]], named after the chemist **Melvin Calvin**. With the energy from the batteries, the plant assembles carbon from CO₂ into glucose. No need for direct sunlight at this stage, but it depends entirely on what the light has produced before.
To follow the path of carbon in the leaf, Calvin used radioactive isotopes from research on the atomic bomb. Nobel Prize in **1961**.
Around **2.4 billion years ago**, photosynthetic bacteria, **cyanobacteria**, began to massively release oxygen. This is the **Great Oxidation**. For many organizations of the time, it was poison.
Then oxygen allowed the ozone layer and much more efficient respiration. The air we breathe is, basically, the “waste product” of billions of years of photosynthesis.
About **half** of Earth's oxygen comes from phytoplankton in the oceans, not just forests.

sections.title: A modest output, an immense role

blocks.text: A leaf only converts **1 to 3%** of the solar energy received into biomass. On a global scale, this is enough to feed food chains and absorb enormous quantities of CO₂.

Hence the interest in forests, oceans… and even artificial photosynthesis for the climate. A sea slug, *Elysia chlorotica*, goes so far as to “steal” chloroplasts from algae to live a little on solar energy.
Photosynthesis transforms light, water and CO₂ into sugar, and regenerates oxygen. It is solar cooking at the basis of almost all life.
